Build log · Dell Precision 5820 · Aug 2026

Precision 5820 Field Notes

Two Tesla V100s in a workstation that refuses to POST with them, cooled by a fan header the kernel cannot see, serving a 27B model to the local network. Every number here was measured on the machine.

Chassis Precision 5820 Tower, board 002KVM CPU Xeon W-2135, 6C/12T GPU 2 × Tesla V100 32 GB BIOS 2.48.0

Chapter 01

The machine, and why it fights back

A workstation Dell sold for CAD, asked to do something Dell never validated.

The Precision 5820 is a single-socket Xeon W tower from Dell's professional line: six cores, 61 GiB of RAM, two NVMe drives, a 950 W supply, and four chassis fan headers wired to an embedded controller nobody outside Dell has documented. It is a good machine. It is not a machine designed to hold two 250 W passively-cooled datacentre GPUs.

That distinction is the whole story. Every problem in this document comes from the same root: a Tesla V100 is a server part, and this is a workstation. The card expects a chassis that pushes air through it and firmware that can place a 32 GB memory aperture. It got neither.

Chapter 02

Three power cycles and a black screen

The failure was easy to reproduce and almost impossible to read.

Install one V100. Press power. The machine cycles itself three or four times, then settles into a black screen and stays there. No Dell logo. No GRUB. No network — the router shows no lease and ARP never resolves. It never reaches POST at all.

The hard part was not the failure. It was that two independent problems were wearing the same costume. A video-routing fault — Primary Video had been pointed at an empty slot — meant nothing reached the monitor even when firmware was perfectly healthy. Underneath it sat the real POST failure. For a while, every experiment produced the same black screen for whichever of the two reasons happened to apply.

Dead end that cost hours

"The fans are steady" is not a POST indicator on this machine. Fans spin up and hold at a constant speed whether firmware completed or hung three seconds in. Reading that as success produced a confident, wrong conclusion that a single V100 had POSTed fine — and sent the investigation down a driver-and-kernel-parameter path for hours.

What actually works, headless: the power-button blink code (solid white = S0, no fault; 3-2 = PCI/video) and a USB keyboard's Num Lock LED, which only responds once firmware has initialised USB.

The way out was to stop testing against a moving baseline. An RTCRST jumper clear wiped NVRAM, every BIOS setting was re-applied by hand, and the machine was verified good with only the display card: Dell logo shown, Ubuntu booted, SSH reachable, both NVMe visible. Then — and only then — the V100 went in.

No Dell logo. One variable, one result. Everything OS-side was now provably irrelevant, because the machine was failing before any OS existed.

Chapter 03

Four bytes of firmware

Dell kept the variable functional and removed the menu that sets it.

A V100 needs a 64-bit prefetchable MMIO window large enough for its 32 GB BAR1. The window is configured by a UEFI variable called SocketCommonRcConfig, and Dell ships it with both the base and the size set to zero — which disables the window entirely, even with "Memory Map IO above 4GB" enabled in Setup. The variable still works. The menu item that would set it was removed.

Reading it requires extracting the BIOS from Dell's PFS container — which is why UEFITool and IFRExtractor find nothing useful on the raw .exe — and then writing four bytes back from a UEFI Shell.

Do not copy another machine's payload

This board's bytes 12–13 are 08 06 — different from the BIOS defaults (00 00) and different again from the 7920T (06 06), and its DataSize is 115 bytes against the 7920T's 114. Pasting a payload from another model corrupts platform topology. Dump your own variable, edit your own bytes.

With the window enabled, the card enumerates properly and the aperture appears at full size:

Writing it

From a UEFI Shell booted off a FAT32 stick. Dump first, edit your own bytes, then write the whole payload back:

One booby trap worth knowing: entering BIOS Setup can reset this variable. Apply all Setup changes first, write the variable second, and don't go back in.

The NVRAM-clear jumper is the undo path, so a bad write is physically recoverable — but on this board the jumper block sits underneath the graphics cards. Reaching it means pulling both V100s first. That is worth knowing before you write anything, not after: the recovery procedure is not a two-minute reach into the case, and there is no video output at all with the cards installed.

Chapter 04

The fan the kernel could not see

Five headers on the board. Four in sysfs. The missing one cools the GPUs.

Dell's fans are driven over SMM BIOS calls — there are no memory-mapped fan registers on this board, and Dell publishes no SMM datasheet. The command codes come from reading the Linux dell-smm-hwmon driver: 0x00a3 get state, 0x01a3 set state, 0x02a3 read RPM, 0x04a3 nominal speed.

The driver declares DELL_SMM_NO_FANS 4, so it never issues a call for fan index 4. Precision Tower boards have five connectors. The fifth — centre position, silkscreened FAN_HDD — is physically the PCIe/GPU cooling fan. It cannot appear in sysfs no matter what is plugged into it, because nothing ever asks the controller about it.

An LKML patch raises the constant to 5 and adds the channel: five insertions, one file, tested on a Precision 5810. Its stated motivation is verbatim this project's problem — the PCIe/GPU fan being uncontrollable with high-power passive GPUs. Building it out of tree and registering it with DKMS makes the fifth channel real.

Making it survive kernel upgrades

The module is in-tree, so an out-of-tree build has to outrank the shipped one. DKMS handles this with a destination path that depmod searches first — Ubuntu's /etc/depmod.d/ubuntu.conf declares search updates ubuntu built-in, and updates wins.

And then the machine stopped booting again

With the fan hub finally under control, the next reboot hung before the bootloader and beeped. No network at all. The cause was a tach reading: 14451 RPM against a nominal maximum of 5100. The control loop ignores tach entirely — but the BIOS reads the same tach during its POST fan check and rejects it.

This is invisible until the first reboot, because everything works perfectly at runtime. An implausible fan5_input is not cosmetic; it is the early warning for a machine that will not boot.

The fix was a slower reference fan on the hub's first port, matched to the channel's nominal ceiling. It solves POST, and it solves a second problem too: the controller runs a closed loop on tach, raising duty until it sees the RPM it expects. Give it a fan that can never reach that number and it drives every fan on the shared hub to maximum, permanently.

Chapter 05

What the embedded controller actually does

A three-state interface wrapped around a controller that is not three-state.

The Linux driver presents fan speed as a 0–255 PWM value, which is a fiction. The SMM interface takes a two-bit state — off, low, high, auto — and the driver's multiplier is 128, so writes quantise to three usable settings. Anything between them does not exist.

That quantisation is a property of the interface, not the hardware. The controller owns the real PWM generators and drives arbitrary duty. The proof was already in the probe data: in automatic mode, three of four channels sit at an RPM that no manual state can produce.

Reading the channel

Also unavailable on this board: GET_TEMP_TYPE (0x11a3) and GET_FAN_TYPE (0x03a3) both fail, so no tempN_label files are created and cat fan1_label returns EINVAL. Which sensor is ambient and which fan is the video fan cannot be asked — only inferred from behaviour.

Which raised the real question: does that continuous curve respond to a hot GPU? A six-minute experiment answered it — sixty seconds idle, then a 470 W dual-GPU soak taking both cards from 35 °C to 62 °C, then four minutes of cooldown, logging every fan and every thermal sensor at five-second intervals.

The answer, and it is unambiguous

Nothing ramped. Nothing decayed. The GPU channel moved 0.23 % under half a kilowatt of load. Meanwhile the sensors the controller could plausibly be watching barely moved: one crawled 30 → 35 °C, another 28 → 30 °C, and a third sat at exactly 25 °C for the entire six minutes without changing once.

The embedded controller cannot see GPU temperature, and nothing downstream of it will cool these cards. Custom fan control is not an optimisation here — it is the only thing standing between two passive 250 W cards and their thermal limit.

One measurement inverted an assumption that had gone unexamined. The GPU channel at manual LOW runs 989 RPM; the controller's own automatic duty runs 2210. LOW is less than half of doing nothing. A conventional fan curve with a sensible-looking floor would have made cooling worse than leaving the service uninstalled.

So the curve became binary and the floor became a hand-back: below a threshold the channel is returned to the controller, at or above it the channel is driven to HIGH. Two useful states, not three, and the useless one is never selected.

The controller does not let go

Setting a fan state is not the same as owning the channel. Because this board is not in the driver's whitelist, the command that genuinely disables BIOS fan control is never sent — so the EC continues to regulate underneath us. It reverts a commanded speed within seconds, and the control loop commands it again.

On the GPU header this shows up as a slow sag between writes, cured by asserting once per second instead of once per five. On a plain chassis header it is far worse: that fan cycled between 716 and 2869 RPM continuously while the controller pulled it back toward its own tach target and the loop pushed it up again.

A conclusion that did not survive

The chassis fan looked, for one run, like it was worth 1.9 °C — and that number went into the notes. It was wrong. That run happened to start three degrees cooler in ambient than the run it was compared against, and while the fan was oscillating it cooled no better than not running at all.

What was actually being measured was steady airflow, which the GPU header delivers on its own once it is asserted every second. The second fan was dropped.

Chapter 06

Finding the plateau

Every early run aborted at a limit set below the machine's normal operating temperature.

The safety watchdog killed any workload reaching 63 °C — a deliberate margin chosen while the cooling was unproven. It also meant that for weeks, every soak was being terminated at exactly the moment it reached steady state. Runs that looked like thermal failures were healthy runs hitting an arbitrary ceiling.

Raising the limit and letting the workload run to completion produced the numbers the whole build had been waiting for.

The counter-intuitive result is in the middle two rows. Single-GPU runs 9 °C hotter than split, despite putting less total heat into the chassis — roughly 290 W against 500 W. The chassis sensor reads the same in both cases.

The explanation is duty cycle. Layer-split runs the cards sequentially, so each alternates between 250 W and 50 W and averages around 150. Pinning to one card holds it at a sustained 250 W. Die temperature follows per-card duty, not the heat going into the case — which also means chassis airflow improvements buy far less here than intuition suggests.

The benchmark was pessimistic — by nine degrees

Every figure above comes from a synthetic benchmark, which drives a continuous stream with no idle. Loading the actual serving endpoints with real requests instead gives 66.2 °C, against 75.3 °C for the same two cards under the benchmark.

The reason is duty cycle: across the run the cards were above 200 W for only 77 % of samples, and combined draw averaged 389 W rather than the ~500 W the benchmark sustains. Real requests have gaps — client round-trip, the transition from prefill to generation, a slot falling idle. So the measurements that shaped every cooling decision here were conservative, and the machine in service sits 16.8 °C inside spec.

Fitting an exponential to the rise curve turned out to predict the plateau well. From 51 seconds of noisy data the fit gave 64.9 °C; the measured plateau was 65.4 °C. The second, slower pole — chassis air warming over minutes — contributed about 2 °C, not the ten a cautious reading had allowed for.

Chapter 07

Choosing a model

A benchmark that won decisively, and lost anyway.

Generation on these cards is memory-bandwidth bound — proven early, when splitting a model across both GPUs gave a 34 % prefill improvement and exactly zero generation speedup. That points hard toward a mixture-of-experts model, which activates only a fraction of its parameters per token and therefore moves far fewer bytes.

A 30.5B MoE with 3.3B active parameters was pulled and benchmarked against the installed dense 27B. On speed it was not close.

Then the accuracy numbers arrived

The dense model already installed scores 77.2 % on SWE-bench Verified — within four points of a frontier commercial model, and better than a 397B model from the same family. The MoE scores around 50–52 %.

A 3.5× speedup bought at the cost of roughly 27 points of coding accuracy is not a trade worth making. The MoE was a generation older and already marked deprecated upstream; its architecture was doing exactly what the theory predicted, but it was the wrong instance of that architecture.

Even matched generation-for-generation, the pattern holds: the same family's MoE variant scores 73.4 % against the dense 77.2 %, described upstream as four times faster and four to twenty points worse. The literature agrees — MoE wins decisively at matched active parameters, dense wins at matched total parameters, and factual capacity tracks total weights.

The benchmark was not wasted. It established what MoE does on this specific hardware — 120 t/s, 178 W, single-card identical to split — so when a current-generation coder MoE appears, only the accuracy question remains open.

Chapter 08

Serving it

One instance per GPU, and no load balancer in front.

Two independent servers, each pinned to its own card, each holding a full copy of the weights. Splitting the model across both cards was measured and rejected: for a per-GPU instance it gains nothing and adds cross-card traffic.

Context sizing came from measuring rather than guessing. Loading at two different context lengths separates the fixed cost from the per-token cost:

Why there is no load balancer

The server caches the KV state of the previous prompt per slot. A request landing on the same instance as the previous turn skips prefill entirely. A full 128K re-prefill costs about 140 seconds.

Round-robin would destroy that cache on every single turn — far more expensive than any imbalance it corrects. Two agents, two ports, assigned directly. Sticky routing by client IP fails here too, since both agents run from the same machine.

One model-specific detail worth carrying: this is a reasoning model, and by default it fills a separate reasoning field while leaving the standard content field empty until it finishes thinking. Most OpenAI-compatible clients ignore the reasoning field and read that as a broken server. Disabling it server-side, with per-request opt-in for clients that want it, was verified working in both directions.

Chapter 09

Bugs that reported success

The costly failures all had the same signature.

Nothing in this build was hard because it was obscure. The expensive problems were the ones where a tool said "done" and the effective state was different.

The config that was silently ignored

A restart limit was set to stop a failing service from retrying forever. It was written into the wrong section — systemd moved those directives in v229 and ignores them where they were placed, falling back to a ten-second window that a ten-second restart delay can never fill. The service was configured to fail visibly and would in fact have retried indefinitely. The unit file looked correct. Only asking the running system what value it ended up with revealed it.

The arithmetic that was concatenation

Port numbers were computed as a base plus an instance index. systemd does no arithmetic in unit files, so 8080 and instance 0 became port 80800 — above the 65535 limit. Both instances failed to start. Install reported success.

The variable that changed under privilege

A build script wrote its output relative to the home directory, unprivileged. The install step ran under sudo, where the home directory is root's. The two halves disagreed about where the artefact lived, and the tool reported "no module built" for a module it had just built successfully.

The dependency that deleted itself

A fan-control service was declared as wanted by the system's main startup target, and — carelessly — also ordered to start after that same target. That is a cycle, but nothing complained, because for weeks nothing else referred to the service.

Then the model servers were given an ordering dependency on it, so they would not start before cooling was running. That closed the loop. The init system resolved it the only way it can: by silently deleting the model servers' start jobs. No failed unit. No error. Both units still reported themselves as enabled and intending to start. The only trace anywhere was a single line:

The part worth carrying: this class of bug cannot be reproduced by restarting the service. The cycle only exists while the startup target is doing the starting. Every manual restart during development worked perfectly. It took an actual power cycle to surface, on a machine that had by then been reconfigured a dozen times without one.

The readback that lied

The attribute reporting whether a fan channel is under manual control returns "automatic" even while a manual state is in force — because the driver never actually disabled automatic control on this board, so the controller truthfully reports its own mode. Trusting it made the control loop issue two firmware calls per channel per cycle where one would do, and a fan began oscillating. Of the three attributes the driver exposes for fans, only the measured RPM can be believed: one returns "no data" in the normal case, one silently clamps to a fixed value, and this one reports the opposite of the truth.

The self-inflicted one

Killing a background download by matching its command line also matched the SSH command doing the killing, terminating the session. This happened four times across the project, and it is documented in the project's own notes. Remembering harder was not the fix; not using pattern-matched process kills from a remote one-liner was.

The habit that catches all of them

Writing the configuration is not evidence the configuration took. Ask the system what it actually ended up with — query the property, read the effective value, probe the channel — before believing the write succeeded. Every bug above survived a successful-looking write and died the moment something inspected the result.

Chapter 10

Doing this yourself

A runbook, in dependency order, with a verification gate on every stage.

This is written to be followed with an AI coding agent driving the machine over SSH, because that is how it was done. The agent is good at the tedious parts — parsing sysfs, writing systemd units, running telemetry loops. It is not good at knowing when a plausible answer is wrong, which is why every stage below ends in a check that either passes or does not.

Read this before anything else

Never reuse another machine's firmware payload. The variable in Chapter 03 is board-specific: this one is 115 bytes with 08 06 at offset 12, the sibling workstation is 114 bytes with 06 06. Writing another model's bytes corrupts platform topology. Dump your own, change the four bytes that matter, write your own back.

Have the case open and know where the NVRAM-clear jumper is before you write anything. That jumper is the entire undo path.

Stage 0 — before you touch it

Hardware: a display card (the Xeon W has no integrated graphics, so without one you cannot see POST at all), a FAT32 USB stick with a UEFI Shell at /EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI, a USB keyboard, and a fan solution for the cards — passive Teslas have no fan and will not survive on chassis airflow alone. Record your BIOS version and confirm it is one you trust; a newer one is not automatically better.

Stage 1 — establish a known-good baseline

Clear NVRAM, re-apply every BIOS setting by hand, and boot with only the display card. Do not skip this. Debugging a POST failure against a machine that has a second, unrelated fault is how weeks disappear.

Gate: vendor logo appears, OS boots, SSH reachable, all drives visible. If any of those fail, you are not yet debugging the GPU problem.

Stage 2 — the firmware window

Install one accelerator. If it does not POST, dump the variable from a UEFI Shell, identify the MMIO base and size fields, set them, write back, and verify by re-dumping. Apply all Setup changes first — entering Setup afterwards can reset the variable.

Gate: lspci -v shows the card's large BAR at its full size and 64-bit prefetchable. Anything less means the window is still wrong.

Stage 3 — find every fan channel

Count the physical headers on the board, then count fan*_input entries in sysfs. If the board has more, the driver is capping. Rebuild it, register with DKMS, and build for every kernel in /lib/modules — not just the running one.

Gate: the new channel appears, and probe on it visibly moves the fan you expect. A channel that appears but moves nothing is wired elsewhere.

Stage 4 — reboot before you trust it

Everything can work perfectly at runtime and still fail POST, because firmware reads the tach during its own fan check and rejects implausible values. This is invisible until the first reboot.

Gate: a full power cycle reaches the OS with the fan hardware connected. If the machine beeps and hangs, the tach is out of range — fit a reference fan whose maximum matches the channel's nominal ceiling.

Stage 5 — measure before you write a curve

Do not assume the controller ignores your GPUs and do not assume it responds. Log every fan channel and every thermal sensor through an idle → load → cooldown cycle and compare each channel's load-versus-idle delta against its own jitter band. Measure what each manual state actually delivers in RPM before choosing any of them as a floor — on this board the "low" preset moves less air than doing nothing.

Gate: you can state, with numbers, what every fan state delivers and whether automatic control responds to GPU load.

Stage 6 — find the plateau, then set the limit

Run a sustained load for several thermal time constants — long enough that the curve flattens, not just long enough to look alarming. Set your safety cutoff above the measured plateau. A cutoff below normal operating temperature turns every healthy run into a false alarm.

Gate: a workload runs to completion and the temperature is flat for the last third of it.

Stage 7 — choose the model on accuracy, then check it fits

In that order. Benchmarks measure speed, which is the easy half; a model that is three times faster and materially worse at the job is not a win. Establish the quality target first, then check VRAM by loading at two context sizes and solving for the per-token cost.

Stage 7b — reboot before you believe any of it

Restarting a service is not the same as booting. Ordering between units, module loading, device naming and firmware checks all behave differently when the startup target is driving, and several failures exist only in that path. Power-cycle the machine and confirm every service comes up with nothing typed afterwards.

Gate: after a cold boot, no failed units, the accelerator fan channel present, both endpoints listening, and — specifically — journalctl -b | grep "ordering cycle" returns nothing.

Stage 8 — serve it, then verify from another machine

One instance per accelerator, each pinned, each holding its own copy. Key in a file rather than on the command line. Firewall scoped to your subnet. Then test from a different host — an unauthenticated request should be refused, which proves reachability and enforcement in one call.

Working with the agent

Three instructions are worth giving explicitly, because each corresponds to a real failure in this build:

Ask the system what it ended up with. Writing a config is not evidence it took effect. Query the effective value, read the channel back, probe the result.

Distinguish measured from assumed. Insist that any number in a recommendation is traceable to a command that produced it, and that extrapolations are labelled as such. An estimate from a 20-second sample of a throttled download is not a measurement.

Never pattern-match process kills over SSH. A command containing a filename will match the shell running it. Use recorded PIDs and marker files.
